blocks.title: Learning Outcomes
items: Recognize LabVIEW fundamentals: controls, indicators, VIs, SubVIs, data types, arrays, clusters, loops, and shift registers.
Create a LabVIEW VI that calculates voltage-divider output.
Measure how photoresistor resistance changes as light level changes.
Use a voltage divider to convert resistance variation into voltage variation.
Wire a sensor to Arduino A0 and an LED to digital pin 7.
Program an automatic lighting system using a threshold decision.

blocks.title: Build the Voltage-Divider VI
paragraphs: Build a [LabVIEW VI](kb:vi-subvi) that represents and evaluates a [voltage-divider circuit](kb:voltage-divider). Create an appropriate [front-panel interface](kb:front-panel), add the required [controls and indicators](kb:controls-indicators), and construct the corresponding [block-diagram logic](kb:block-diagram).

blocks.alt: Completed LabVIEW voltage-divider front panel with Vin, R1, R2, Vout, Stop, student name, and student ID
blocks.caption: Example completed front panel. Keep controls, indicators, labels, and wiring guides arranged clearly.

blocks.title: Beginner Build Sequence
items: Start a blank VI. A VI is the LabVIEW program file; it has a front panel for the user interface and a block diagram for program logic.
On the front panel, place three **numeric controls** named `Vin`, `R1`, and `R2`. A control supplies a value to the program.
To create the boxes and arrows shown in the image, use the **Controls >> Decorations** tab.
Place one **numeric indicator** named `Vout`. An indicator displays a value calculated by the program.
Open the block diagram and use [arithmetic functions and wires](kb:program-elements) to implement `Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2)`. Wires carry data from controls through functions to the indicator.
Place the calculation inside a [While Loop](kb:while-loops), add a Boolean `Stop` control, and wire it to the loop Stop terminal.
Run the VI, change the three inputs, and confirm that `Vout` updates. End the program with the Stop control, not the Abort button.
Add your name and student number to the front panel, then save the file with the `.vi` extension.

blocks.title: Why the While Loop is used
paragraphs: The While Loop repeatedly updates the voltage-divider calculation and keeps the front panel responsive while the VI runs. It continues until the programmed Stop condition is met, so the student can change inputs without pressing Run again. Stop the VI with its Stop control rather than the Abort button.

blocks.alt: LabVIEW block diagram showing an empty While Loop and the Functions palette path to the While Loop structure
blocks.caption: Place the While Loop from the Programming > Structures palette, then build the repeated calculation inside its border and connect a Stop control to the loop condition.

blocks.prompt: Which formula should the VI implement?
blocks.hint: The output is the input voltage multiplied by the lower resistor fraction.
blocks.explanation: The VI should calculate Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1 + R2).

blocks.title: Build Steps
items: In Tinkercad, select New, then Circuit.
Find a photoresistor in the component list.
Place it so its two legs are in separate breadboard rows.
Add a multimeter and connect the meter leads across the two photoresistor legs.
Set the [multimeter mode](kb:multimeter) to Resistance.
Record measurements at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% light.

blocks.title: [Why the Divider Matters](kb:voltage-divider)
paragraphs: The [photoresistor](kb:photoresistor) changes resistance with light. The [Arduino analog input](kb:analog-input) reads voltage, so the divider converts resistance variation into a measurable sensor voltage.

blocks.title: Divider Rule
blocks.note: In this sensor sequence, the fixed resistor is 4.7 kΩ and the photoresistor changes with light.

blocks.title: Circuit Steps
items: Add the fixed resistor so it shares one row with the photoresistor junction.
Set the resistor value to 4.7 kΩ.
Connect one end of the divider to 5 V and the other end to GND.
Connect Arduino 5 V and GND to the same power rails used by the divider.
Measure the divider junction voltage relative to ground.
Set the multimeter mode to Voltage.

blocks.title: Table 2 - Divider Voltage
blocks.note: Record measured voltage at the same light levels used in Table 1.

blocks.prompt: What resistor value is used in the simulated divider?
blocks.hint: This value appears in both the Tinkercad divider and real hardware exercise.
blocks.explanation: The divider uses a 4.7 kΩ resistor.

blocks.prompt: Why add the voltage divider before Arduino sensing?

options.text: It turns photoresistor resistance changes into voltage changes the Arduino can read.
It prevents the LED from using digital pin 7.
It replaces the need for ground.
It makes the photoresistor resistance constant.

blocks.hint: Arduino analog inputs measure voltage, not resistance directly.
blocks.explanation: The divider converts photoresistor resistance variation into a voltage variation.

checkpoints.title: Connect and Program the Automatic Lighting System

blocks.alt: Photoresistor and LED connected to Arduino

blocks.title: Connection Steps
items: Delete the multimeter.
Connect the divider junction to Arduino Analog Input A0.
Add the LED and a 220 Ω current-limiting resistor in series.
Connect the LED circuit between Arduino digital output pin 7 and ground, using the correct LED polarity.
Before running code, confirm common ground is shared by the divider and LED circuit.

blocks.title: Program and Verify
items: Click Code at the top right of [Tinkercad](kb:tinkercad).
Change edit mode from Blocks to Text.
Enter the automatic lighting sketch.
Start the simulation and change light level.
Confirm the LED turns on when the sensor reading is below 400.

expected.message: Confirm the LED turns on below the low-light threshold before completing this stage.

options.text: J7 to A0, LED output to digital pin 7.
J7 to D7, LED output to A0.
Photoresistor to digital pin 13, LED to A5.
Both photoresistor and LED to GND only.

blocks.hint: The sensor voltage goes to an analog input; the LED is controlled by a digital output.
blocks.explanation: J7 connects to A0, and the LED is controlled from digital output pin 7.

blocks.prompt: What does the provided code do when PR is below lowLightLim?

options.text: It turns the LED on by writing HIGH.
It turns the LED off by writing LOW.
It changes PRPin from A0 to A1.

blocks.hint: Read the if statement: PR below the limit enters the first branch.
blocks.explanation: When PR is below lowLightLim, the code writes HIGH to the LED pin.
